title: Lighthouse AI - Private Deployment network & egress discovery
summary: Initial discovery focused on private/VPC deployment requirements. Main topics: VPC peering vs private endpoints, egress restrictions for EU/US workloads, firewall/NAT requirements, KMS integration for model keys, audit logs, and SLA expectations. Customer requested security docs and an architecture checklist and offered to share their network diagram.
action_items: Ava: send SOC2 + private deployment security whitepaper and private deployment checklist by 2027-06-06
Devon: prepare a rough network diagram example showing Private Endpoint + peering flow and suggested firewall ports by 2027-06-07
Maya: share Lighthouse AI internal network diagram and list of AWS accounts/regions by 2027-06-08
Samir: confirm data residency requirement (EU-only for PII workloads) and share list of restricted regions by 2027-06-09
next_steps: Schedule a technical deep dive with networking team week of 2027-06-14
Run a quick smoke benchmark on Redwood Dedicated (small pilot) if network design is validated
Share pricing/commitment options for Dedicated vs Private once capacity and region constraints are clarified
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-04 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~59 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Devon (Redwood SE), Maya, Samir, Evelyn, Jonas (joined 00:12)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): Customer evaluating Redwood for private model serving behind company VPC. Key constraints: some workloads must remain EU-only, some teams ok with US. They need KMS integration, audit logs, and strict egress policies.

[00:00] Ava: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're excited to talk through private deployment options for Lighthouse. quick introductions?
[00:12] Maya: yeah hi i'm maya head of infra, i'll kick off, we run most services in AWS, multi-account org, want to avoid public internet egress for inference for certain models.
[00:22] Samir: Samir here, security architect. main ask: keys written in our KMS, audit trail to our SIEM, and egress locked down to only a set of regions.
[00:30] Devon: great thanks, Devon here from Redwood, i'll be the technical lead — i can walk through vpc designs, private endpoints and peering patterns.
[00:40] Evelyn: Evelyn, cloud eng — i'm most interested in routing, nat gateways, and how retries/failover would happen across regions.
[00:50] Ava: perfect, we'll start with a high level, then dig into the network patterns — peering vs private endpoints — and then region/egress constraints and security integrations.

[04:10] Devon: so at a high level we offer a Private deployment option that can run in your VPC (private control plane + customer dataplane) or in our managed clouds with private endpoints. two common patterns: one, VPC peering/transit where Redwood pods sit in a managed VPC and you peer; two, Private Endpoint (like AWS PrivateLink) so traffic never traverses public internet.
[04:35] Samir: can you clarify the difference re: egress? if we peer with Redwood's VPC, do we still have to allow outbound internet?
[04:45] Devon: good question. with peering, egress depends on where the model serving is — if it's in Redwood's managed VPC, any external calls (e.g., to telemetry or external model stores) need egress rules on Redwood side or we can route via your NAT; with PrivateLink, the interface endpoint appears in your subnet and the traffic is between your ENIs and Redwood, so less public egress. the tradeoff: peering gives lower latency for large KV cache transfers but requires routing table updates and sometimes route propagation; private endpoint reduces your exposure to public IPs but may have per-GB charges.
[05:20] Maya: hm, our security lead prefers PrivateLink-ish approach, but we have a bunch of legacy IP allow lists that expect peered CIDRs. also some of our infra can't accept interface endpoints easily due to cross-account routing.
[05:35] Devon: that's common. we've done hybrid: control plane via private endpoint, dataplane via dedicated peered subnets in your account (or in our dedicated account but peered) and you can restrict egress at the subnet level. we've also supported transit gateway patterns for large orgs.

[07:10] Ava: timeline wise — what are you evaluating for — do you want a pilot in eu-west first?
[07:20] Jonas: sorry i'm late — CTO jonas. yes, we want to keep EU production models in eu-west-1. US can be on hosted for now. we also need to understand SLA and failover — if eu-west goes down do we failover to us or keep offline?
[07:35] Samir: for PII models we cannot fail over to US automatically — policy is manual failover only and logs must be retained in EU.
[07:45] Devon: we can pin model versions and create routing policies so EU traffic stays in eu-west-1; automatic fallback to a different region is configurable but can be disabled for specific models. logs can be exported to your S3 in eu-west and to your SIEM via our audit log stream.

[10:00] Evelyn: regarding ports and firewall — what port ranges do we need to open for peering vs private endpoint?
[10:12] Devon: for PrivateLink it's TCP 443 (https) to the interface endpoint; for peering we typically use a set of ports — 443 for control plane, and for gRPC/tcp for inference we often use 10k-11k range for data plane (but that's configurable). we'll provide a port matrix.
[10:34] Maya: do you require NAT for egress to pull model artifacts or images from ecr / public buckets?
[10:40] Devon: if your dataplane pulls from your accounts (private ECR) it uses peered routing, no NAT. if it needs to pull from public endpoints, you'd either allow egress via NAT on the peered subnet or we can mirror images into your privated repo.

[13:20] Samir: KMS — we need customer-managed KMS keys for any model keys. do you support HSM integration or bringing your own key?
[13:30] Devon: yes we support external KMS/HSM. for Private deployments we can use your KMS in the account for encrypting model artifacts and runtime keys. HSM integrations are available for enterprise, we need to coordinate key policies.
[13:50] Maya: great, is that available for Redwood Dedicated as well or only Private?
[13:55] Devon: both but Dedicated (reserved capacity) often uses a dedicated pool where we can integrate per-customer KMS and keep artifacts in their S3. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you the most control.

[16:05] Ava: what's your expected throughput/latency for production? helps sizing.
[16:12] Jonas: for the chat model — 10 qps sustained with p95 latency under 300ms for short responses; for embedding workloads it's batchy, 1000s per minute.
[16:24] Devon: ok that maps well to a small dedicated pool with autoscaling. for low-latency p95 around 300ms we'd recommend GPU based serving (A100 or cheaper quantized options), and we'd configure KV cache warmers. note that private peering may reduce network overhead which helps latency.

[19:00] Samir: audit logs and retention — can you stream logs to our S3 in eu-west with at least 1 year retention?
[19:12] Devon: yes we can push audit events to your S3 or forward to your Kinesis/CloudWatch/Splunk endpoint. retention controlled on your side. we also have a console with token-level tracing if you want to sample traces.

[21:45] Maya: compliance: do you have SOC2 and ISO certs? and do you provide a penetration test report for Private deployment?
[21:55] Ava: we are SOC2 Type II and have ISO alignment docs. for Private deployments we provide architecture review templates and can share pen test summaries under NDA. i'll attach the security pack after the call. (link: https://redwood.ai/security-whitepaper)

[24:10] Evelyn: cross-account peering — we run workloads across 5 accounts. is there a recommended pattern?
[24:20] Devon: many customers use a central transit account or transit gateway and attach their workloads. Redwood can peer with that central account or with a dedicated Redwood account. we can also create interface endpoints per account if needed. take into account route table scales and ASG limits.

[28:00] Jonas: about costs — any surprising network charges for private endpoints?
[28:10] Ava: PrivateLink often has per-GB data processing charges; peering typically has cross-az/region data transfer costs depending on your cloud. we'll include a cost comparison for your expected throughput. Redwood Optimize can also suggest quantization to reduce token costs.

[32:35] Samir: what about egress policing — we need to limit destination CIDRs to a tiny set (e.g., only our SIEM ingest, artifact repos). can we do that?
[32:45] Devon: yes, you can restrict egress at the subnet/NACL level and we support an allowlist for external callbacks. for telemetry we can route telemetry to your collector via private peering. if you want zero public egress we recommend a design where artifacts are mirrored into your account and all external integrations are proxied by your infra.

[35:50] Maya: are there any limitations on region availability for certain models?
[35:58] Devon: some GPU families or pre-built quantized variants may only be in certain regions at first; we publish a model-region availability matrix. if a model variant isn't in eu-west we can either replicate the model to eu-west or run it in a compatible CPU/quantized path — but you'll see performance tradeoffs. this is where Dedicated + model pinning helps.

[39:20] Evelyn: for pilot, what's the minimal setup to validate latency and e2e connectivity?
[39:28] Devon: minimal pilot: 1) mirror one model artifact into a customer S3 in eu-west; 2) create a private endpoint or peering to a small dedicated pool; 3) run synthetic qps (10 qps) and measure p95/p99. we can do this in 1-2 weeks once we have network access and IAM roles.

[42:00] Jonas: we have strict data residency for PII — we'd like an attestation that data won't leave eu-west for those models. is that possible?
[42:08] Ava: we can provide contractual language in the enterprise addendum to require data residency and forbid cross-region fallback for named models. we'll loop legal after the technical design.

[45:15] Samir: monitoring/alerts — if there's a change in routing or egress, can we get an automated alert?
[45:24] Devon: yes, Redwood Console supports alerting on route anomalies and token-level latency spikes. for network changes we recommend CloudWatch/QRM alarms on your Transit Gateway/route tables and our tracing webhooks.

[48:50] Maya: do you store any user prompts or outputs? we need to ensure no retention beyond what's necessary.

[49:00] Devon: by default logs are sampled and you can configure retention. for Private deployments, logs stay in your account if you request it, and you can control retention via S3 lifecycle. we also support a no-retention policy for specific models.

[52:10] Ava: wrapping up, i'll summarize the key decisions we need: 1) choose peering vs private endpoint (they prefer PrivateLink but need to confirm cross-account), 2) confirm EU-only list of models and no-auto-failover, 3) share network diagram and allowed CIDRs, 4) agree pilot scope and timing.

[54:00] Jonas: sounds good. next steps: we will share diagram and policy, and schedule the deep dive with our network team.
[54:15] Ava: we'll send security pack, port matrix, and a sample architecture plus proposed pilot plan.
[54:25] Devon: i'll also draft a minimal config for the private endpoint setup and a peering fallback pattern.

[58:30] Ava: thanks all. closing notes: expect docs in 48-72 hours and we'll set up the follow-up meeting.
[58:45] Maya: thanks, appreciate it.

End of transcript.
